Named by the Woodward Royal Commission as associated with the organisation responsible for the 1977 disappearance and killing of Donald Mackay
One conviction, a 1978 fine for tax offences; no conviction for the Mackay killing

content.p: Robert Trimbole, known as Bob, was a Griffith mechanic who became a marijuana wholesaler in the Riverina and Sydney in the 1970s. The Sydney Crime Museum calls him one of the most violent and successful of Sydney's criminals for much of that decade. He was never convicted of the killing that his name is most often linked to, the 1977 disappearance of the Griffith anti-drugs campaigner Donald Mackay. He was fined in 1978 for tax offences, and that was his only conviction, according to the Australian Dictionary of Biography. He died in Spain in 1987, ten years after Mackay vanished.

Trimbole was born on 19 March 1931 in Griffith, the fourth surviving child of Italian-born parents who had come from Plati in Calabria. He trained as a motor mechanic in Sydney and married Joan Quested in 1953. Back in Griffith he leased a garage, but in 1968 he was declared bankrupt after a tax debt. The garage burned down with its records. He was discharged from bankruptcy in 1975.

The Dictionary of Biography says that early in the 1970s Trimbole was already organising the supply of marijuana to a growing Sydney market, and that a Melbourne stand-over man, Gianfranco Tizzoni, managed distribution of Griffith's crop in Melbourne from 1971. The trade depended on bribed police and officials. In 1972 Trimbole bought a steakhouse and a butchery in Griffith, sold both a year later, and moved to Lansvale in south-west Sydney, where he bought a supermarket and a liquor store.

The Sydney Crime Museum describes the Griffith growers as wealthy men who built large houses in the district, which became known as "grass castles". It says the returns from marijuana were very large per acre, and that Trimbole later moved into trucking, wholesale wine and a supermarket. The museum also says he had a long interest in horse racing and at one stage kept 13 jockeys on his payroll. The Dictionary of Biography says that by the late 1970s his wealth could not be disguised, and that he claimed to be a successful punter while laundering money through gambling.

Donald Bruce Mackay was born in Griffith in 1933 and ran a furniture business there. He stood unsuccessfully as a Liberal Party candidate for the State seat of Murrumbidgee in 1973 and 1976, and for the federal seat of Riverina in 1974. While campaigning he became concerned about marijuana at Griffith, and the Dictionary of Biography says he passed information to the Sydney Drug Squad. That information led to a raid on 10 November 1975 on a plantation at Coleambally, where police found what the Dictionary of Biography calls the largest single crop yet discovered in Australia.

The Age reported in 2012 that Mackay had told a reporter two days before he vanished that he believed he was a marked man. He had feared that local police were protecting the Griffith mafia, a fear that was borne out years later when three police stationed at Griffith were jailed for perverting the course of justice. The Age also reported that the drug squad had used his furniture store as a secret headquarters for the operation.

The Age reported in 2011 that a drug squad detective was forced to hand his notebook to the defence in the court case over the plantation, and that Mackay's name was in it as the informant. The Crime Library archive says the notebook was sworn as evidence and read out in open court.

On the evening of Friday 15 July 1977, Mackay left the Hotel Griffith after an after-work gathering and vanished. The Dictionary of Biography puts his departure at about 6.30 p.m. His bloodstained vehicle was found about seven hours later in the hotel car park, still locked, with its keys on the ground, according to The Age. Three spent small-calibre cartridges lay nearby. His body has never been found.

The Crime Library archive reports that, several months earlier, an unidentified man had tried to lure Mackay to Jerilderie with a promise of a large furniture order. Mackay was detained on another matter and sent an employee in his place, and the meeting did not happen. The archive quotes Woodward's finding that the appointment had been part of a plan to ambush and dispose of him.

The Dictionary of Biography says that the outcry over the missing man prompted Premier Neville Wran to create a royal commission under Justice Philip Woodward. The Canberra Times described the cannabis plantations Mackay had warned about as so extensive that the state needed the commission. The Sydney Crime Museum says that a campaign at first pushed the idea that Mackay had run off with a lover, and that a retired corrupt police officer, Fred Krahe, told journalists so.

Woodward's report was delivered in 1979. The Dictionary of Biography says he concluded that Trimbole was "the practical leader" of a marijuana operation that, in his view, was behind Mackay's death. The Crime Library archive reports that the suspect list was whittled down to seven names, including Trimbole, Bazley, and George Joseph and Tizzoni, whom the archive calls two associates of Trimbole.

In the official transcript quoted by the Crime Library archive, Woodward said he had named Trimbole as associated with marijuana production in Griffith and as the director of an operation at Euston, and that he was, if not the top man in the Griffith district, one of them. The same archive records Woodward's finding that "the disposal of Mackay was the result of an organized plan". Woodward said Mackay was disposed of by the organisation he found to exist in Griffith. The Daily Advertiser quotes the same finding: Mackay was disposed of by members of that organisation at Griffith on 15 July 1977.

The Daily Advertiser, reporting on the 2017 funeral of Griffith figure Tony Sergi, quoted the same finding and noted that Woodward had described Trimbole, with Sergi's cousin Pat Sergi and others, as responsible for distributing the product and sending the profits back to Griffith. The same report noted that the commission had called Tony Sergi "The Operator", and that Sergi was alleged to have ordered Mackay's killing.
James Bazley was convicted in 1986 of conspiring to murder Mackay, as described below.
content.h2: Mr Asia and the flight from Australia
content.p: The Dictionary of Biography says that after Mackay's disappearance Trimbole made himself available to the Mr Asia heroin syndicate, which had recently arrived in Sydney from New Zealand. Its account lists his distribution network, his contacts in the police and customs, a stock of blank birth certificate forms, and an ability to organise killings. In 1979 he is said to have spent time in London, helping the syndicate as it struggled in Britain, under the names Bob Jones and Bob Taylor.

The Sydney Crime Museum says that in the late 1970s Trimbole met the syndicate's leader, Terry Clark, at the races. It says he arranged the killing of the couriers Douglas and Isobel Wilson after they became police informers. The Dictionary of Biography says that at the 1980 inquest into the Wilson couple's deaths in Victoria, Trimbole was let off giving evidence, as his answers could have incriminated him. The museum adds that he may have been involved in many more killings, and it puts the possible number as high as 18. The museum states this as suspicion, not as a finding, and no other account gives that figure.

In May 1981, the Dictionary of Biography says, Trimbole flew out of Australia on a tip-off, shortly before the Commonwealth government announced a royal commission into drug trafficking under Justice D. G. Stewart. The Sydney Crime Museum says he fled when the Stewart inquiry was announced, and that he suspected he would be arrested over Mackay's killing. The two accounts agree on the timing but describe his reason in different ways.

According to the Dictionary of Biography, Tizzoni was caught in 1982 when police found marijuana in the boot of his car. He then won a lighter sentence by admitting he had found the gun and the gunman for the killing, and he said he did so at Trimbole's behest. Trimbole was never tried over that account.

Trimbole was found living in Ireland under the name Michael Pius Hanbury. He was jailed in October 1984 on suspicion of possessing a firearm. A judge later found that the arrest had been illegal. Australia and Ireland had no extradition treaty at the time, and he flew out of Ireland on a charter aircraft the day he was let go in February 1985.

The Dictionary of Biography gives his death as 13 May 1987, apparently of a heart attack, at a villa near Alicante in Spain. He had been living there with Ann-Marie Presland, whom he had lived with since 1973, and her daughter. The Trimbole family brought his body back to Sydney for a funeral Mass at St Benedict's Catholic Church in Smithfield, and he was buried beside his parents at Eastern Creek cemetery. Presland, his two daughters and his two sons survived him.
The Sydney Crime Museum says he died six years after leaving Australia, and that he appears to have been successful in hiding most of his fortune.

Melbourne underworld figure James Frederick Bazley was convicted over Mackay's death. The Dictionary of Biography says that in 1986 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for conspiracy to murder Mackay, and that he protested his innocence. The Age reported that Bazley was also found guilty of murdering the Wilson couple and of taking part in a $270,000 armed robbery, and that he was released in 2001 after serving less than 15 years. Bazley has denied being the killer. The Age reported that he told the crime reporter Tom Prior that the killer was a New South Wales policeman, Fred Krahe, who died decades ago. That is Bazley's own claim, reported by The Age, and no court has found it true.

The Dictionary of Biography notes that a 1987 special commission of inquiry into the police investigation named police officers, politicians and members of the Society. In 2012, the New South Wales police offered a reward of $200,000, double the earlier figure, for information leading to Mackay's remains. The Age reported that the reward was now for information leading to the remains, not to a conviction, and that investigators had privately conceded it was unlikely anyone would be charged outright. Investigators believed Mackay was assassinated on the orders of Griffith-based kingpins, including the late Trimbole. The Age also reported that Mackay's wife, Barbara, died in 2001 without knowing where her husband's body was.

In 2013 the Canberra Times reported a police search of a property near Hay for the remains. Its commentary said that even if the remains were found, the circumstances of the death might never be fully explained.

Mackay's disappearance is one of Australia's most notorious cold cases, according to the Canberra Times. The Sydney Morning Herald, writing in 2017, argued that the names linked to the Mackay killing kept appearing in later organised crime cases. It noted that Francesco Barbaro, named by the Woodward inquiry as a leading figure in the cell responsible for the killing, was followed by a son, Pasquale Barbaro, who was arrested in 2008 over a large ecstasy import and who was gunned down in a Sydney street in November 2016, aged 35. The Sydney Crime Museum says Pasquale Barbaro was arrested in 2008 with 19 others over a shipment of ecstasy hidden in tomato tins, and that the Woodward inquiry linked his father to Trimbole.

Mackay's four children have never known what happened to their father's body. Trimbole died in 1987, and the Sydney Morning Herald wrote in 2017 that for the Mackay killing the silence may never be broken, and that the full truth of what happened in Griffith that night may never be known.
